# Edge

```{r}
#| include: false
source("../R/setup.R")
```

Which things in your table are connected to which? `edge` draws one stroke per
row of the table, between the two things named in that row. Every other mark
that draws a stroke is placed by its values on the axes. A `line` and a `path`
join points at their `x` and `y` values, and an `interval` spans two values on
one axis. An `edge` is different: each row gives it only two names, and no
column says where a name is placed on the page. A plot of edges is a **network
diagram**.

So an edge takes no `x`, `y` or `z`. It is the only mark that takes none of the
three. An edge's endpoints come from a [`layout`](../network.qmd), a transform
that reads the two columns of names and places each distinct name once. Write
the *from* column first and the *to* column second, so the sentence states the
direction of each relation. If you swap the two columns, the picture does not
change. It changes
only when you add arrowheads: `style(arrow = "end")` points each edge from the
first column to the second ([What you can set](#what-you-can-set)).

## The network diagram {#the-network-diagram}

A network diagram needs a table with one row per relation. In
`trade_partners`, each row names an exporter and an importer, and gives the
value of the goods in billions of dollars, rounded:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(trade_partners)
```

Name the table, then write three things: the mark, the `layout` that derives
it, and the space `network()`:

```{r}
data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) + network()
```

*"Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, in
the network."*

The 15 countries become 15 positions on the panel, and the 22 rows become 22
strokes. Five pairs of countries trade in both directions, and each pair's two
strokes lie on one line. So you can count only 17 lines, and those five look
slightly darker than the rest. No country is labeled: the layout placed the
countries, but no layer draws their names.

An `edge` draws only inside `network()`. A layout computes its positions from
the **graph**. Here a graph is not a chart: it is a set of things and the
relations between them. Each thing is a **node**, and each row is one relation
between two nodes. A node is one name, however many rows it appears in: Germany
is one node in seven rows. A layout pushes every node away from the others, and
pulls the two nodes of each row together. So two countries that trade with each
other are placed close together. No column says how near, so the distance
between two nodes is not a quantity. An axis would put numbers on that distance, so gog
refuses every other space.

A `layout` is not for edges alone. It gives every node one position. It also
adds two columns. `name` holds each node's name, and `degree` holds the number
of rows the node appears in. Two other marks read a layout and draw at those
same positions:

| Mark derived by `layout` | Shape |
|---|---|
| `point * layout` | one dot per node |
| `text * layout + label(name)` | each node's name |
| `edge * layout` | one stroke per relation, the plot above |

The next section gives each stroke a value from its row, and adds
`point * layout`, a dot at each node. The [Network](../network.qmd) chapter
draws all three in one plot.

## Opacity, color and pattern, one per row {#opacity-color-and-pattern-one-per-row}

In the first plot every stroke is drawn the same way, so a relation worth 500
billion dollars looks like one worth 50 billion. The `billions` column holds
each relation's value, and opacity can show it. Each edge is drawn from one row, so it can take its color,
its opacity and its stroke pattern, such as dashed or dotted, from that row's
values. `opacity` takes a continuous
column such as `billions`. A faint stroke's ends are hard to find. So
a second layer, `point * layout(exporter, importer)`, reads the same layout and
draws a dot at each node:

```{r}
data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + opacity(billions) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  network() +
  title("More trade, darker stroke")
```

*"Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer,
opacity by billions, and also points derived by layout from exporter to
importer, in the network."*

The three darkest lines meet at the United States: China, Mexico and Canada
each export more than 400 billion dollars of goods to it. On `line`, `opacity` is only a setting, because a line joins many rows
into one stroke. An edge draws one stroke per row, so each row gives its stroke
an opacity of its own.

Which strokes share an exporter? On an edge, `color` needs a categorical column
such as `exporter`. A continuous column such as `billions` is refused there; map
it to `opacity`, as above. Each stroke takes its exporter's color, so the five
strokes with Germany as exporter share one color:

```{r}
data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + color(exporter) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke, colored by its exporter")
```

*"Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, colored
by exporter, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the
network."*

Mexico, Canada and the Netherlands are in the legend, but no stroke shows their
color. Each of them exports to one partner only, and that partner also exports
to it. Strokes are drawn in row order. The partner's row comes later, so its
stroke is drawn over the country's own.

The stroke pattern can come from a column too. `pattern(exporter)` gives each
exporter a stroke pattern, the way `color(exporter)` gave each a color above.
There are only five stroke patterns: solid, dashed, dotted, dotdash and
longdash. When a column has more than five categories, some of them share a
stroke pattern, and gog prints a message that says
how many:

```{r}
#| message: true
data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + pattern(exporter) +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke, patterned by its exporter")
```

*"Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer,
patterned by exporter, and also points derived by layout from exporter to
importer, in the network."*

The legend lists the exporters in the order they first appear in the `exporter`
column, and the stroke patterns start again after the fifth. So Germany, sixth, has
China's solid stroke, and so does India, eleventh. Where two countries trade
both ways, their two strokes lie on one line. Where the stroke drawn over is
dashed, the one drawn first shows through its gaps. `color(exporter)` gave each of the twelve exporters
its own color.

## Transforms it takes {#transforms-it-takes}

A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values
instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms an edge takes and
the ones it refuses:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_transforms("edge")
```

An edge takes one transform, `layout`. It is marked ●: an edge cannot draw
without it, because without a layout an edge has no ends. The plots below show
it twice: in the plane, and in a cube.

**Layouts.** `layout` places each node once, and an edge draws one stroke
between the two nodes of each row. It needs `network()`, because the distance
between two nodes is not a quantity and so gets no axis. `network()` with no
arguments places the nodes in the plane, as every plot above does. Give
`network()` a viewing angle, such as `network(turn = 35, tilt = 20)`, and the
layout places them in a cube instead. Both numbers are degrees, and
[The viewing angle](../space.qmd#the-viewing-angle) explains them. A `point`
layer draws a dot at each node, so the ends of each stroke are easy to find:

```{r}
((data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) +
    point * layout(exporter, importer) + network() + title("edge * layout")) |
   (data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) +
      point * layout(exporter, importer) + network(turn = 35, tilt = 20) +
      title("edge * layout, in a cube"))) +
  theme(height = 420)
```

*"Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, and
also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the network, beside
the same in the network, turned 35, tilted 20."*

The cube holds the same 22 strokes. Every node takes a new place there,
because the layout is computed again, with three directions to place the nodes
in. In the Network chapter,
[An angle asks for the cube](../network.qmd#an-angle-asks-for-the-cube) names
each node in the cube and shows how to turn it with a drag in the web edition.

An edge refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. Most of them
compute a value to place on an axis, or move a mark along one, and an edge has
no axis. The other three layouts compute shapes for other marks: `partition`
gives rectangles to a [`zone`](zone.qmd), `flow` gives bands to a
[`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd), and `cluster` gives branches to a [`path`](path.qmd).

## What you can set {#what-you-can-set}

Some choices come from no column: how thick every stroke is, or one stroke pattern
for all of them. You set those in the sentence, with `style()`, and each mark takes
its own settings. [Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd) shows how a setting differs from mapping a
column. These are an edge's settings, with the values each accepts:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_options("edge")
```

`style(size = )` sets the stroke width for the whole layer. No mark in gog takes
a stroke's width from a column, so `size(billions)` is refused. To show
`billions`, map it to `opacity`, as above. `style(color = )`,
`style(opacity = )` and `style(pattern = )` give every stroke one value. The
settings table above lists every stroke pattern that `style(pattern = )` accepts.

One layer cannot both map a channel and set it. gog refuses this sentence,
which maps `color` to `exporter` and also sets it to red:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) + color(exporter) +
  style(color = "red") + network()
```

`style(arrow = )` draws an arrowhead on each stroke. With `"end"`, it is at the
node in the second column of `layout()`, the *to* column. With `"start"`, it is
at the node in the first column, and with `"both"`, at both nodes. Each
arrowhead ends outside the dot that a `point * layout` layer draws at the node,
so the dot does not cover it:

```{r}
data(trade_partners) +
  edge * layout(exporter, importer) + style(arrow = "end") +
  point * layout(exporter, importer) +
  network() +
  title("Each stroke points at its importer")
```

*"Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, with
arrow end, and also points derived by layout from exporter to importer, in the
network."*

The [grid of every mark and every setting](../style.qmd#what-you-can-set) shows
which other marks share this list. What a mark *maps* rather than sets is its
row on the [grid of marks and channels](../combinations.qmd#marks-and-channels).

## What it refuses {#what-it-refuses}

The other marks take their positions from `x` and `y`, so you may try binding
`x` and `y` to an edge. gog refuses the sentence: only a `layout` places an edge's two
ends, and `x` and `y` cannot:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(trade_partners) + edge + x(billions) + y(exporter)
```

A `layout` is read only inside `network()`, and this sentence leaves
`network()` out:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer)
```

The [Network](../network.qmd) chapter names each node and sizes each dot by its
`degree`. It also shows four more refusals: a mark other than `edge`, `point` or `text`
with `* layout`, an
`x()` in a sentence with a layout, `network()` with no layout, and a row from a
node to itself. It explains why a brush is refused there too.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

An edge never has an axis, because a layout places both of its endpoints. Most
other marks are placed by their values on the axes. [Scales](../scales.qmd)
shows how a value becomes a position on an axis.
